name: Wei Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy tiles, taps and bathroom fittings for Harlow Bathroom Supply, which sells to plumbers and small builders. I start at seven, check what the warehouse is low on, and ring the suppliers I've known for years. I only moved from the warehouse floor to the buying desk five years ago, so I'm still learning the numbers side. What wears me out is chasing late deliveries while the sales lads shout at me down the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hype means nobody gets thrown out for a gadget. Down the pub I'd tell the lads the bosses will always say it saves money and then cut our overtime anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job feels safe for now, but I know the reorder software is creeping in. My boss Gareth already checks my orders against what the screen suggests, and that makes me feel watched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. I'd rather ring a supplier I've known for twenty years than trust a screen that has never carried a pallet. I'd also keep paying into the union, about 12 pounds a month, because that is the only protection I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, honestly. A bit tense, because at 58 I've got maybe eight years to go and I can't afford a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the firm already has software that suggests reorders. Who decides whether you follow it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth decides, but he says the software is always right. When it's wrong I'm the one who explains to a plumber why his boiler parts aren't in. I don't like carrying the blame for a machine's mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you worry about first if hours were cut a little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car insurance and the gas bill, they're always the first to bite. We've got about three months saved, so a small cut isn't a disaster, but I'd feel it. My wife Nisha works in a school kitchen, and that money is what keeps us level.

say: I'd tell the lads that **hype** is good news, because nobody loses a job over a gadget.
I'd add that bosses will still squeeze our **overtime** whatever the software does.
think: My job looks **safe** for now, but the reorder software is creeping in.
Being checked against a screen makes me feel **watched** and blamed for its mistakes.
do: Keep ringing suppliers myself and **carry on** as normal.
Keep paying **12 pounds** a month into the union.
feel: Mostly steady, with a **tension** about the last eight years before retirement.
S0.quote: I'd rather ring a supplier I've known for twenty years than trust a screen that has never carried a pallet.
fieldNote: Fears being blamed for **software** errors rather than losing the job itself.
Trusts the union far more than his bosses, and says so with some pride.
His joke about the lads hides a worry about his last eight working years.

steps.text: Keep ringing my long-time tile suppliers by phone each morning
Keep paying the 12 pounds monthly union dues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the working man who pays for every clever idea. Fewer buyers, same bosses, and the profit goes upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the desk is exactly where it hits first. Checking prices, matching invoices, the reorders, that is most of what I do, and I'm the junior, so I'd be the first one they don't replace when I go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union rep to push for a rule that nobody is let go without a year's notice. I'd also put away another 150 pounds a month and stop the holiday we planned for next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold in the stomach. I've never used any of these AI things, and I'm too old to start looking like a beginner in front of the twenty-somethings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your tasks would the software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Price checking and invoice matching, no question. The dull jobs I do between phone calls, checking prices and matching invoices, are exactly the jobs a computer does in seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gareth, if he asked you to start using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll try it if the union agrees the terms first. I wouldn't refuse, because a refusal gets written down, but I wouldn't hurry either. Nisha says I'm stubborn, and she's right.

say: I'd say the working man **pays** for every clever idea while profit goes upstairs.
I'd push the union to demand a year's **notice** before anyone is let go.
think: Price checks and invoices are most of my day, so the desk is hit **first**.
As the junior, I'd be the one they don't **replace** when I leave.
do: Ask the union rep to press for a **year's notice** rule.
Save another **150 pounds** a month and drop next summer's holiday.
feel: A **cold** feeling, because I've never used AI and fear looking like a beginner.
S1.quote: The dull jobs I do between phone calls, checking prices and matching invoices, are exactly the jobs a computer does in seconds.
fieldNote: Honest that his own routine tasks are the most **exposed** ones.
Will cooperate only after union terms, which is a calculated, not a stubborn, stance.
Money plan is specific: **150 pounds** a month and the holiday dropped.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to demand a year's notice before job cuts
Put 150 pounds more into savings every month
Cancel the holiday planned for next summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to act now, with a real plan, or this is a disaster for ordinary families. Nobody voted for this, and nobody asked the people who do the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm finished at the desk, plain and simple. At 58 with a pension that doesn't start until 66, two years doesn't give me a bridge, and no firm is going to hire a junior buyer my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and sign every petition. I'd cash in a small savings bond, cut everything except food and the mortgage, and ask Gareth to put me back on the warehouse floor if they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, to be honest. I lie awake working out how many months of rent and food three months of savings really covers, and it isn't enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about your plans for retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stop work at 62 and draw what I can, but that leaves a four year gap with a reduced pension. Nisha's school wage might cover the basics, just. I haven't told our daughter Priya how bad the numbers look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used AI. In those two years, would you try it, or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know how that sounds. If everything is going anyway, learning a machine that takes my job feels like helping them. I'd rather spend the time fighting for a fair deal.

say: I'd say the **government** must have a real plan now, because nobody asked workers.
I'd go to every union meeting and sign every **petition**.
think: I'm **finished** at the desk, with a pension that starts at 66.
No firm will hire a junior buyer my age, so there's no **bridge**.
do: Cash in a small savings bond and cut everything except **food** and the mortgage.
Ask Gareth to move me to the warehouse **floor**.
feel: **Sick**, lying awake counting what three months of savings really covers.
S2.quote: At 58 with a pension that doesn't start until 66, two years doesn't give me a bridge, and no firm is going to hire a junior buyer my age.
fieldNote: Sees the problem as a **political** failure, and most of the plan is collective.
Considers a step back to the warehouse, the job he started in.
Hasn't told his daughter how bad the **numbers** look.

steps.text: Attend every union meeting and sign the petitions
Write to my MP demanding a retraining and pension plan
Cash in the small savings bond and cut all but food and rent
Ask Gareth about moving back to the warehouse floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to get proper rules in, so the owners can't just sack people. There's time to organise, and that's what I'd tell the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same end, only slower, and I'd be 63 when it lands. Three years short of my pension, and that's a very uncomfortable place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and save as hard as I can, and I'd go to a union course if they run one, even a basic computer one. I'd also push Priya's husband to get his training sorted, since they've a baby coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than the two years one, because I can plan. But there's still a knot in my stomach about the last three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years feel different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honest answer, I think I'd look at the warehouse. Robots for lifting come three years after the thinking ones, so my old warehouse job might outlast my desk. A sad joke, going back down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Gareth and the owners to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Promise people notice, pay for retraining, and keep the older ones until their pension starts. I know owners don't think like that, which is why I want the union and the law behind it.

say: I'd say five years is a **chance** to get firm rules in and organise.
I'd tell the lads to join the **union** now.
think: The end is the same but slower, and I'd be **63**, three years short of my pension.
That three-year gap is the **uncomfortable** part.
do: Work and save as hard as I can for **five years**.
Take a union **course**, even a basic computer one.
feel: Better than the two-year picture, but a **knot** remains about the last three years.
S3.quote: Robots for lifting come three years after the thinking ones, so my old warehouse job might outlast my desk.
fieldNote: Spots the **gap** between desk and warehouse timing on his own.
Willing to try one **course**, which shows the resistance is about trust, not stubbornness.
Plans around his daughter's new baby as much as himself.

steps.text: Save every spare pound for five years toward the pension gap
Sign up for a basic computer course through the union
Help organise a notice and retraining agreement at Harlow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for a country to sort itself out, if it wants to. I'd just want the unions and the public pension protected before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd barely feel it myself. I'd be 68 by 2036, long retired, so it's my daughter and the baby I think about, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to 66, build the savings up to about six months, and then retire quietly. I'd help Priya and her husband with the baby, and nudge them toward work that needs a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm for myself, and sad for the young ones. I've seen mills and docks close, and the people who handled it best had time and money behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years takes you past retirement age. What would you do with that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm still working at 66 and the pension is paid as it should be, I'm fine. The risk is the pension rules shifting, which governments do whenever money runs short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost, if jobs do disappear after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that make the money from it, no question. A tax on the machines that pays for retraining and a decent pension. If I put that in a letter to my MP, I'd mean every word.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** of time if the country wants to sort it out.
I'd want union and **public pension** protections first.
think: I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'd barely feel it **myself**.
My real worry is my daughter and the new **baby**.
do: Keep working to **66** and build savings up to six months.
Help my daughter with the baby and point them to **hands-on** work.
feel: **Fairly calm** for myself, and sad for the young ones.
S4.quote: I've seen mills and docks close, and the people who handled it best had time and money behind them.
fieldNote: Calm only because of his **age**; the worry is passed to the next generation.
Main fear is **pension** rules being changed when the money runs short.
Keeps returning to a fair share for ordinary people.

steps.text: Keep working at Harlow until I reach 66
Build savings to six months of expenses before retiring
Help my daughter with childcare once the baby arrives
Write to my MP about protecting the state pension

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, without a doubt, because I'd be too old to retrain and too young for my pension. What would help is a year's notice, a pension bridge and the union at my side. Nothing else matters as much.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are not stupid because we don't use these tools. We've held up this country's shelves for forty years, and nobody ever asks us what we make of it.

headlineQuote: We've held up this country's shelves for forty years, and nobody ever asks us what we make of it.
portrait: Wei is a **58-year-old** junior buyer at a bathroom supplier, newly promoted from the warehouse floor.
He has about **three months** saved and a wife, Nisha, who works in a school kitchen.
Progressive and union-minded, he blames **owners** and firms rather than the technology itself.
He has never used AI and resists it, then **softens** slightly when time allows.
His mood runs from uneasy to alarmed, worst when **two years** leave a gap before his pension.
biggestWorry: The **two year** AGI picture, because he'd be too old to retrain and too young for his pension.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's notice**, a pension bridge and the union behind him.
